LeadFlow / Case study

Closing the handoff gap between online sales and stores

A workflow prototype for automotive DTC lead management: who owns a lead, whether they accepted it, and what happens next.

Role: Product design & prototyping
·
Timeline: October–November 2026
·
Tools: ChatGPT, Codex

02

The CRM has the lead. Who owns the next step?

Online appointment staff can qualify leads, invite customers to stores, and pass them to sales advisors. LeadFlow explores what happens when the CRM records the reassignment, but the context and follow-up still have to be passed separately.

  • Reassigning a lead is a field change. Nothing confirms the receiver accepted it.
  • Customer context — a promised Saturday test drive, a child seat — sits in chat history, not in the record.
  • Open follow-ups don't move with the lead, so after a handoff nobody owns the next step.
  • Supervisors export to Excel to find stuck handoffs and uneven workloads.

LeadFlow is a prototype of this handoff layer. It is not a CRM replacement; in production it would ship as a module inside the existing CRM.

03

Evidence

Public job descriptions provide two signals about the work. They describe expected responsibilities; they do not establish how often handoffs fail.

  1. Online qualification and store assignment

    Leapmotor’s DCC specialist posting lists qualifying online leads, arranging store visits, assigning qualified leads to sales advisors, and maintaining follow-up records.

    Employer job posting · Leapmotor

  2. Handoff notes and continued follow-up

    Huajue Group’s DCC posting describes inviting prospects for a test drive, following up with people who do not arrive, and passing high-intent leads to sales advisors with handoff notes.

    Employer job posting · Huajue Group
04

Four rules the workflow enforces

01

Handoffs must be accepted

A lead changes owner only when the receiver accepts it, so a handoff can't silently go nowhere.

02

Tasks move with the owner

Open follow-ups migrate to the new owner together with the customer's context.

03

Every active lead has a next step

An active lead without a next task is flagged; the supervisor dashboard tracks this at zero.

04

Timeouts escalate

Handoffs not accepted in time, and overdue tasks, surface on the supervisor dashboard with drill-down to the exact leads.

05

Decisions and trade-offs

  1. Accept-to-own instead of direct reassignment

    Alternative considered
    Let senders change the owner directly
    Why
    Direct reassignment is faster but makes it impossible to tell a received lead from a dropped one.

  2. On duplicate merge, keep the original owner and status

    Alternative considered
    Let imported data overwrite
    Why
    Imports shouldn't silently take a customer away from the salesperson already working with them; imported fields are kept in the batch record.

  3. Reactivated leads don't count as new acquisition

    Alternative considered
    Count them as new leads
    Why
    Counting them would inflate acquisition numbers and hide churn.

  4. Unassigned leads can only be at early stages

    Alternative considered
    Allow any stage in the pool
    Why
    A customer who has test-driven or bought must always have a responsible person.
06

Getting existing data in

Stores keep historical leads in Excel. The import flow maps columns automatically, validates each row, catches duplicates against existing leads, and sends unowned leads to the supervisor's pool.

Demo sample: 6 rows → 2 invalid, 1 duplicate, 3 new

07

What this is — and isn't

  • Prototype with fictional data; actions are stored only in the browser.
  • Not connected to a real CRM, DMS, or service records.
  • Metrics I'd track in a pilot: median handoff acceptance time, share of active leads with no next step, overdue tasks per salesperson.

First pilot: ask an online coordinator, a store advisor, and a supervisor to walk through the same appointment handoff using their current tools and the prototype. Check whether the receiver can identify the owner, promised appointment, and next action without asking the sender. Use their current handoffs as a baseline before testing acceptance time and overdue follow-ups.

08

How I built it

I prototyped the workflow with ChatGPT to validate the flow quickly, then used Codex to fix data consistency and add the Excel import. The goal was to test workflow rules with something clickable, not to ship production code.

I started with the ownership decision: who is responsible before and after acceptance? I then built a demo around one Saturday test drive, added the supervisor’s exception view and spreadsheet import, and replayed the journey with fictional data. The project records span October to November 2026.
